body.hook: Advanced band music has signs that send you back, forward and around: D.S. al Coda, first and second endings, key changes in the middle. Miss one and you're playing a different part of the piece from everyone else.

study.title: Reading the Road Map
study.question: How do I navigate complex music on the first read?
study.passage:
Advanced sight-reading checklist (written for this lesson):
1. Title, composer, style marking: what character is the music?
2. Key signature and any key changes later (look for double bar lines with new sharps or flats).
3. Time signature and any meter changes.
4. Tempo and tempo changes (rit., accel., a tempo).
5. Road map: trace with your finger: repeats, first and second endings, D.C., D.S., Fine, To Coda, Coda.
6. Rhythms: find the hardest bars and count them.
7. Dynamics and articulations: note the biggest changes.
8. Accidentals.
Road map practice: a teacher-made one-page piece: A section with repeat and 1st/2nd endings; B section; D.S. al Coda; coda. Trace the order and write it as letters: e.g. A(1st) A(2nd) B A-to-coda Coda. Then sight-read it in pairs.

body.objective: Students will be able to read complex rhythms.
successCriteria: I can count sixteenth-note patterns with "1 e & a"
I can count triplets and compound metre
body.hook: Sixteenth notes, triplets, 6/8 and cut time: these rhythms show up in grade-level band music and can make sight-reading feel impossible. With the right counting system, they become patterns you recognize instantly.

vocabulary.definition: A quarter of a beat in 4/4, counted "1 e & a."
Three equal notes in the space of two, counted "1 trip let."
A metre where each beat divides into three, such as 6/8.
Six eighth notes per bar, felt in two beats of three.
Recognizing common rhythm shapes at a glance.

study.title: Complex Rhythms Decoded
study.question: How do I count complex rhythms quickly?
study.passage:
Counting systems (written for this lesson):
Sixteenths in 4/4: "1 e & a 2 e & a." Common patterns in one beat: four sixteenths (1 e & a); eighth + two sixteenths (1 & a); two sixteenths + eighth (1 e &); dotted eighth + sixteenth (1 a).
Triplets: three eighth notes in one quarter-note beat: "1 trip let, 2 trip let."
6/8: six eighths grouped 3 + 3; count "1 2 3 4 5 6" slowly or feel 2 big beats ("1 la li 2 la li") at faster tempos. Dotted quarter = one big beat.
Cut time: same notes as 4/4 but the half note gets the beat; count "1 & 2 &" where each count is a quarter note. Marches are often in cut time.
Activities: 1. Flash cards: name and clap rhythm patterns on sight. 2. Clap a sixteenth-note line with the metronome on quarters. 3. Play triplets against a duple beat. 4. Read the same melody in 6/8 at slow (6 beats) and fast (2 beats) tempos. 5. Play a march excerpt in cut time.

body.objective: Students will be able to sight-read in an ensemble.

body.hook: Sight-reading alone is one challenge; sight-reading with a whole band means keeping going while 40 other people are doing the same. It's a key skill for festivals, auditions and honour bands.

vocabulary.definition: The time given before sight-reading to look at the music.

study.title: Reading Together
study.question: How does a band sight-read successfully?
study.passage:
Ensemble sight-reading routine (written for this lesson; modelled on common festival sight-reading formats):
Study time (e.g. 5 minutes): the director talks through key, time, tempo, road map and tricky spots. Players: finger silently, count hard rhythms under breath, and mark nothing unless the rules allow pencils.
Landmarks: note rehearsal letters, long notes and places where your section plays alone. If you get lost, aim for the next landmark.
Recovery rule: if lost, stop playing, follow the music with your eyes, listen for the melody or a landmark, and rejoin on a strong beat. Never stop the band by yourself.
Ensemble awareness: watch the conductor at tempo changes and listen for the melody.
Practice: the band sight-reads two short pieces in festival format. After each, students rate: Did we keep going? Were key and rhythm correct? Where did people get lost?
Reflection: name your landmarks and how you recovered.
